newsitem.title: FRANCE: French assembly votes to end military conscription.
newsitem.headline: French assembly votes to end military conscription.

text.p: France's National Assembly on Tuesday adopted a law ending compulsory military service, introduced by the French Revolution of 1789.
The bill, approved by 435 votes to 97 on a first reading, must still go to the Senate, the country's upper house, where it will be heard next month.
Defence Minister Charles Millon told the lower house it had shown "imagination and audacity" in voting for a move that was "revolutionary....a historic reform".
He said a compulsory five-day "citizen's meeting" to replace the current 10-month-long military duty meant national service was "suspended" but that conscription continued.
The vote was however widely interpreted by the public, and especially by youths, as meaning they were no longer liable for unpopular compulsory army duty.

The reform is part of President Jacques Chirac's plan to eliminate conscript-based units and transform the armed forces into an all-professional organisation, easier to deploy outside France's borders. A sizeable part of the ground forces and most of the navy and air force have been all-professional for years.

The "citizen's meeting," widely seen as a sop to parliamentarians suspicious of professional armies, will entail five days of lectures on patriotism and related topics and give the army a chance to give physical examinations to youths in case compulsory service has to be reintroduced.
